claims.title: The Eastern March granted to the Babenbergs
claims.summary: The marchia orientalis, a frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire on the Danube, was entrusted to Count Liutpold of the Bavarian house of Babenberg, beginning their long rule over the future Austria.

sources.label: Ostarrîchi: Austria under the Babenbergs

claims.title: First mention of 'Ostarrîchi'
claims.summary: A charter of Emperor Otto III used the word 'Ostarrîchi', the 'eastern realm', the earliest recorded form of the name Österreich (Austria), referring to the Babenberg march.

sources.label: Ostarrîchi: Austria under the Babenbergs

claims.title: The Privilegium Minus raises Austria to a duchy
claims.summary: Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa's Privilegium Minus elevated Austria from a march to a duchy and detached it from Bavaria, granting the Babenbergs wide hereditary rights; Vienna became their seat.

sources.label: Ostarrîchi: Austria under the Babenbergs
sources.publisher: Die Welt der Habsburger (The World of the Habsburgs)

claims.title: End of the Babenberg line
claims.summary: Duke Frederick II 'the Quarrelsome' was killed fighting the Hungarians, leaving no male heir; the extinction of the Babenbergs left the duchy of Austria contested among neighbouring powers.

sources.label: Ostarrîchi: Austria under the Babenbergs

claims.title: Battle of the Marchfeld
claims.summary: Rudolf I of Habsburg defeated and killed the Bohemian king Ottokar II near Dürnkrut on the Marchfeld, seizing the Austrian lands; in 1282 he enfeoffed his sons with them, founding Habsburg rule in Austria.

sources.label: The Habsburgs take over Austria

claims.title: First Ottoman siege of Vienna
claims.summary: The army of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna for three weeks in the autumn of 1529 before withdrawing, the first great Ottoman assault on the Habsburg capital.

sources.label: The first Turkish siege of Vienna, 1529

claims.title: Second Ottoman siege and the relief of Vienna
claims.summary: An Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa besieged Vienna until a relief force led by Charles V of Lorraine and King Jan III Sobieski of Poland routed it on 12 September 1683, a turning point against Ottoman expansion.

sources.label: The second Turkish siege of Vienna, 1683

claims.title: Prince Eugene and the conquest of Hungary
claims.summary: After Vienna's deliverance, Prince Eugene of Savoy won victories such as Zenta (1697) and the capture of Belgrade (1717); the Peace of Karlowitz (1699) secured Habsburg control of Hungary and Transylvania.

claims.title: Reign of Maria Theresa
claims.summary: Inheriting the Habsburg lands under the Pragmatic Sanction, Maria Theresa survived the War of the Austrian Succession and reformed the administration, army and education across her dominions.

claims.title: The Empire of Austria proclaimed
claims.summary: In response to Napoleon's imperial coronation, Franz II issued a patent assuming the hereditary title of Emperor of Austria as Franz I, formally constituting the Habsburg lands as an empire.

claims.summary: Franz II laid down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire, which was dissolved after some thousand years, leaving the Habsburg ruler as Emperor of Austria alone.

claims.title: Revolution and the accession of Franz Joseph
claims.summary: The revolutions of 1848 shook the Austrian Empire, drove the chancellor Metternich into exile and brought the eighteen-year-old Franz Joseph to the throne, where he would remain until 1916.

claims.title: The Austro-Hungarian Compromise
claims.summary: The Ausgleich of 1867 reorganised the empire into the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary, two states sharing a common monarch, foreign policy, finance and army; Franz Joseph was crowned king of Hungary on 8 June.

claims.summary: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne, and his wife Sophie were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, the spark that led Austria-Hungary to war.

claims.title: Collapse of Austria-Hungary and the First Republic
claims.summary: As the war was lost the empire disintegrated; Emperor Karl I renounced participation in government on 11 November and the Republic of German-Austria was proclaimed on 12 November 1918, ending Habsburg rule.

claims.title: Treaty of Saint-Germain
claims.summary: Signed for Austria by Karl Renner, the treaty confirmed the breakup of Austria-Hungary, forbade union with Germany without League of Nations approval, limited Austria's army and ceded South Tyrol to Italy.

claims.title: South Tyrol ceded to Italy
claims.summary: Under Saint-Germain the German-speaking southern part of historic Tyrol was awarded to Italy, placing a large German-speaking population under Italian rule and creating a lasting territorial grievance.

claims.title: Dollfuss and the corporate state
claims.summary: Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspended parliament and established an authoritarian 'corporate state'; he was assassinated by Austrian Nazis in July 1934, deepening the First Republic's crisis.

claims.title: The Anschluss
claims.summary: German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938 and on 13 March a law proclaimed reunification with the Reich; Austrian independence ended and a manipulated April plebiscite recorded near-total approval.

claims.title: The Austrian State Treaty
claims.summary: Signed at the Belvedere in Vienna by the four occupying powers and foreign minister Leopold Figl, the treaty restored Austria's full sovereignty and ended the four-power occupation; it came into force on 27 July 1955.

claims.summary: After the last occupation troops left, the Austrian parliament passed a constitutional law declaring the republic's permanent neutrality, the condition on which the Soviet Union had agreed to withdraw.

claims.summary: Following a referendum on 12 June 1994 in which about two-thirds voted in favour, Austria joined the European Union on 1 January 1995, integrating the neutral republic into the European mainstream.
